clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive lysosomal lipid-trafficking disorder caused by biallelic variants in NPC1 (the great majority) or NPC2, impairing egress of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids from late endosomes/lysosomes.

Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, initially affecting downward saccades, is a hallmark neurological sign and should prompt consideration of NPC in any child or adult with unexplained ataxia or cognitive decline.

Presentation is strikingly age-dependent: neonatal cholestatic jaundice with hepatosplenomegaly, infantile hypotonia and developmental delay, or juvenile/adult-onset ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and progressive dementia.

Gelastic cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter) and progressive psychiatric symptoms, including psychosis in adolescents and adults, are characteristic and frequently misattributed to primary psychiatric illness.
Splenomegaly, often isolated and long-standing, may precede neurological onset by years and is a valuable diagnostic clue when reviewing the history.

Diagnosis rests on molecular confirmation of biallelic NPC1/NPC2 variants, supported by plasma oxysterol and lysosphingolipid biomarkers; filipin staining of cultured fibroblasts is a confirmatory functional test.
Substrate-reduction therapy with a glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor can slow neurological progression but does not reverse established deficits, underscoring the value of early recognition.
reference.pathophysiology: Niemann-Pick disease type C is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder of intracellular lipid trafficking rather than a primary enzyme deficiency. Loss-of-function variants in NPC1 (a large polytopic late-endosomal/lysosomal membrane protein) or, less commonly, NPC2 (a small soluble luminal cholesterol-binding protein) disrupt the coordinated handover and export of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids from the endolysosomal compartment. The consequent accumulation of cholesterol, sphingosine, sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids within neurons and reticuloendothelial cells triggers secondary derangement of calcium homeostasis, autophagy and lysosomal function. In the brain this produces progressive neuronal loss, neuroaxonal dystrophy, meganeurite and ectopic dendrite formation, and neurofibrillary tangle pathology, particularly affecting Purkinje cells and cortical and brainstem neurons, giving the characteristic combination of cerebellar, extrapyramidal, oculomotor and cognitive dysfunction alongside visceral (hepatosplenic) storage.
additionalDifferentials: Niemann-Pick disease types A and B (acid sphingomyelinase deficiency)
Gaucher disease type 3 (with horizontal supranuclear gaze palsy)
Wilson disease presenting with movement disorder and hepatic involvement
Adolescent-onset primary psychiatric disorder with neurological soft signs
Ataxia-telangiectasia and other early-onset hereditary ataxias
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for biallelic NPC1 and NPC2 variants
Plasma oxysterol profile (cholestane-triol and related species)
Plasma lysosphingolipid and bile-acid metabolite biomarkers
Filipin staining of cultured skin fibroblasts for unesterified cholesterol
Brain MRI (cerebellar and cortical atrophy, white-matter change)
Ophthalmological assessment with eye-movement recording for vertical saccadic slowing
redFlags: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with unexplained ataxia or cognitive decline
Neonatal cholestasis with hepatosplenomegaly and later neurological regression
Gelastic cataplexy or new-onset psychosis in an adolescent with neurological signs
Rapid neurodevelopmental regression in an infant with visceromegaly
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is strongly age-dependent, with early infantile neurological forms progressing rapidly and often proving fatal in childhood, while adolescent and adult-onset disease follows a more protracted but relentlessly progressive course. Substrate-reduction therapy and meticulous supportive care can slow decline and improve quality of life but do not halt the underlying neurodegeneration.
pitfalls: Attributing adolescent psychiatric or behavioural change to a primary psychiatric disorder and missing the underlying neurometabolic cause
Overlooking long-standing isolated splenomegaly as an early clue years before neurological onset
Failing to test for vertical (especially downward) saccadic palsy, which is easily missed on routine examination
Assuming normal biomarkers exclude disease when NPC2 or atypical variants may give subtler profiles, so molecular confirmation is essential
Delaying diagnosis and therapy, given that treatment slows but cannot reverse established neurological damage
references: Standard textbook of inborn errors of metabolism
International consensus guidelines on Niemann-Pick disease type C
Clinical genetics reference texts on lysosomal storage disorders
management: Start substrate-reduction therapy with miglustat to slow progression of neurological disease
Consider newer disease-modifying agents such as levacetylleucine and arimoclomol where available
Treat seizures with antiepileptic drugs and manage dystonia, tremor and gelastic cataplexy (for example with anticholinergics or a tricyclic antidepressant for cataplexy)
Manage progressive dysphagia with swallow assessment, texture modification, aspiration precautions and gastrostomy feeding when needed, alongside chest physiotherapy
Treat psychiatric and behavioural symptoms, including psychosis, that are intrinsic to the disease

Monitor neurological progression, swallowing and respiratory status, and coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, neurology, speech and language therapy, physiotherapy and palliative care
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
